articles.title: EU-China trade talks grapple with tariffs, rare earths, and export controls - The Brussels Times
articles.summary: EU-China trade talks grapple with tariffs, rare earths, and export controls  The Brussels Times
articles.full_text:
EU and Chinese trade chiefs agreed to hold further talks on tariffs, export controls and market access after meeting in Beijing on 8 – 9 October 2026.
China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao met Maroš Šefčovič, the European Commission’s Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, Interinstitutional Relations and Transparency, for the second meeting of the EU-China Trade and Investment Consultations, the European Commission announced on Friday.
Both sides reaffirmed they would handle differences within World Trade Organization rules and continue work intended to stabilise and make the bilateral relationship “more balanced”, according to a joint statement published by the Commission.
A third ministerial meeting was scheduled for March 2027, with a ministerial video conference planned for January before that.
Hybrid vehicles, rare earths and market access
The EU and China said they would explore the possibility of reducing or eliminating tariffs on certain goods within WTO rules, according to the statement.
The two sides stated they had reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles “in a WTO compliant manner”, while also recalling a guidance document on “price undertakings” in the EU’s battery electric vehicles anti-subsidy case — a process in which companies can agree minimum prices to address subsidy concerns — and said they would continue related procedures.
They also agreed to continue dialogue on access to each other’s markets for medical devices, with the EU welcoming China’s stated effort to increase imports of EU medical devices, including through a matchmaking event during the 9th China International Import Expo.
China said it would accelerate recognition of the “regionalisation principle” for eligible EU member states — a risk-based approach that can limit trade restrictions to affected areas — and both sides agreed to exchange methods and technologies for disease control as they explore lifting restrictions on animal products affected by bluetongue disease.
On export controls, the EU and China said they would strengthen their export control dialogue and increase exchanges on their respective policies.
China said it was willing to continue facilitating export licences for rare earths and permanent magnets to the EU through a fast-track mechanism, while the EU said it would continue working with member state authorities to facilitate specific priority licences to China in “dual-use” sectors — goods that can have both civilian and military applications.
The two sides also said they had reached an understanding to provide advance warning and improve transparency around the listing and delisting of entities under export control procedures.
The statement added that the EU and China would continue work on intellectual property issues through an EU-China Intellectual Property Working Group and strengthen communication on WTO reform.

articles.title: Minister urges ‘drastic’ action to cut reliance on imports amid review of China trade deficit - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Minister urges ‘drastic’ action to cut reliance on imports amid review of China trade deficit  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): The government must take “drastic” action to reduce its reliance on imports and strengthen domestic manufacturing, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.
He said specifically, the government is reviewing products that contribute to Malaysia's large trade deficit with China, including goods that were once made locally.
Johari did not specify the measures being considered or their implementation timeline.
“We have held many engagement sessions with local companies. Although they disagree, we must take very drastic action for the country’s long-term benefit, to protect our economy without depending on countries that we believe could adversely affect our economy as a whole,” Johari said during oral question time in the Dewan Rakyat on Monday.
The trade minister was responding to Datuk Adnan Abu Hassan (BN-Kuala Pilah), who asked about Malaysia’s exposure to trade tensions and new tariffs arising from its concentration on major trade markets, such as the US and China.
Adnan also asked how the government would ensure export diversification developed higher-value added products, instead of merely expanding assembly or processing activities with limited domestic value added.
According to data from the Department of Statistics and the Ministry of Economy, Malaysia had a trade surplus of RM101.5 billion with the US in 2025, and a trade deficit of RM163.4 billion with China in the same period.
In the first eight months of 2026, Malaysia's trade deficit with China stood at RM159.8 billion, the data showed.
In plain terms, Malaysia sells far more to the US than it buys from it, but buys far more from China than it sells to it.
The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry will examine why some products previously made by Malaysian companies were now being imported, and whether domestic manufacturers could resume producing them, he said.
He argued that relying on cheaper imports could undermine local manufacturing capacity. Once domestic factories closed, products previously imported at low prices could become more expensive, he added.
“We can no longer simply allow imports as the easy way out,” Johari said. The government would identify sectors requiring support to produce raw materials and semi-finished goods locally, with small and medium enterprises playing a greater role in supplying exporters.
Responding separately to a supplementary question from Permatang Pauh MP Muhammad Fawwaz Mohamad on domestic value added in electrical and electronics (E&E) exports, Johari cited RM712 billion in E&E exports and RM567 billion in imports last year, resulting in a sectoral trade surplus of about RM145 billion.
For non-E&E products, he cited exports of RM897 billion and imports of RM885 billion, leaving a much smaller surplus of RM12 billion.
Johari said Malaysia’s semiconductor companies should expand beyond conventional assembly, testing and packaging into advanced packaging. He acknowledged that Malaysia’s substantial exposure to E&E exports left it vulnerable to a downturn in the global semiconductor cycle, changes in technology, supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions.
A sharp downturn could trigger inventory adjustments and production cuts, weighing on national exports, particularly if growth in other sectors was insufficient to offset the decline, he said.
“The government’s approach is not to reduce the role of E&E and semiconductors, which are among Malaysia’s competitive strengths. Instead, we are managing the risks of this dependence through three main strategies,” he said.
These comprise strengthening the E&E value chain through activities such as integrated circuit design and advanced packaging; developing other high-value industries and domestic supply chains; and broadening export markets.
